text: Settled in the mid to late 1800s as a rural farming community, Cloverdale is Surrey’s historic centre. It’s named for the clover that grew in Clover Valley, and you can still feel that history on its streets.
Single-family subdivision houses close to four SD36 schools make East Newton the family end of the Surrey market. Locals call one part of it Chimney Hill.

North Surrey isn’t really one neighbourhood. It’s Surrey’s urban north, with Whalley, Guildford and Fleetwood pockets around the Green Timbers Urban Forest. People come here for the City Centre towers and Holland Park more than a village feel.
Small and self-contained, Royal Heights is an enclave whose story is elevation and views over the lowland. Most of the houses around the park date from the mid-1960s.
People often mix them up, but the City of Langley is its own small city of about 10 square kilometres, separate from the Township around it. Its walkable downtown is the big draw.

Named for the river, Salmon River is a rural acreage and farm district. Its Salmon River Uplands designation is there to protect the rural residential character.
Planned since 1979, Walnut Grove is an established planned community in northwest Langley, north of Highway 1. Shops, movie theatres and the Walnut Grove Community Centre make everyday life easy.

Abbotsford is a city of very different pockets: the established Mill Lake and Clearbrook side, Matsqui Prairie farm ground and newer east-side subdivisions. That mix makes sense once you know the city formed in 1995, when Matsqui and Abbotsford joined.

Abbotsford East is the hillside, view side of the city. Established streets along Old Yale Road give way to newer subdivisions on the McKee and Eagle Mountain slopes. In September 2026 it was the city’s largest detached market by listings.

Chilliwack is a full-service valley city that still runs out to farmland at the edges. There’s the Five Corners and District 1881 downtown, hillside neighbourhoods above the valley floor and ALR fields at the fringe. It’s a good fit if you want city services with a rural backdrop.
Heritage courtyard shops and restaurants have revitalized the historic Five Corners / District 1881 core of downtown Chilliwack.

On the east side of downtown, running out toward Prest Road, Chilliwack Proper East is the older grid. The shops and restaurants of District 1881 are an easy walk or a short drive away. With a mix of older houses and newer builds, it’s for buyers who’d rather be central than out in the subdivisions.

Along Sumas Prairie Road, Greendale is rural farm country on the Sumas Prairie side of Chilliwack. Greendale Community Elementary is right in the area, and the Great Blue Heron Nature Reserve on the Vedder River has more than 10 km of trails. People come for acreage, hobby farms and mountain views. Because it’s floodplain farmland, I always have buyers check ALR status and the flood construction level for the exact parcel.

Hammond is Southwest Maple Ridge, the historic corner bounded by Pitt Meadows and the Katzie First Nation to the west and the Fraser River to the south. Its early-1900s commercial area gives it real character.

Mission sits on the north side of the Fraser and combines urban neighbourhoods with rural sub-areas. In September 2026 its medians were the lowest of the communities in its comparison group, so value is part of the story.

Often called Delta’s oldest neighbourhood, Annieville is a quieter pocket in northwest North Delta along the Fraser River. It has big-lot character and an elementary school right in the neighbourhood.
This is central Ladner, named for its school. Families target the Ladner Elementary and Delta Secondary pairing and like walking to village amenities.
Settled and mostly detached, North Delta is a community on the south bank of the Fraser. It’s made up of four sub-areas: Annieville, Nordel, Scottsdale and Sunshine Hills Woods.

Families like Mid Meadows for its two elementary schools, Edith McDermott and Davie Jones, plus the athletic park, the arena and the Fraser River dike trails. It’s the Bonson Road neighbourhood south of the rail line and Hammond Road, overlapping South Meadows along Bonson.

Built around Birchland Elementary at 1331 Fraser Avenue, Birchland Manor is one of north Port Coquitlam’s smallest family pockets. The Prairie Avenue bus loop at Coast Meridian Road is on its west edge.
Near Central Park, the large forested park is at the end of the street, with two SkyTrain stations and Metrotown right beside it.

At Port Moody’s west edge, with Clarke Road and the Burnaby line close behind and College Park Elementary at 300 Princeton Avenue inside it, College Park is a small, settled pocket of houses. It suits buyers who want an established street over a new hillside build.
Forest Glen puts attached buyers one station or one bus from Metrotown, without the Metrotown address. House buyers want the Clinton / Inman school side east of Willingdon.
One of the newer neighbourhoods in the Heritage Mountain area, Heritage Woods is where families target the Aspenwood Elementary and Heritage Woods Secondary pairing.

Coquitlam’s oldest neighbourhood is Maillardville. French-Canadian mill families settled it in 1909 around Fraser Mills, and it grew into the largest francophone community west of Manitoba. That heritage lives on in Festival du Bois, Mackin Park and the new Maillardville Community Centre, and the City’s plan to make Brunette Avenue a walkable, mixed-use village means change is coming too.

Port Moody’s north shore is mostly Pleasantside: older detached streets above and below Ioco Road, with a run of waterfront lots. Old Orchard Park has the city’s only saltwater swimming beach, the Shoreline Trail runs to Rocky Point, and Sasamat Lake and Belcarra Regional Park are just up the road. The City keeps it low-density because of Ioco Road traffic, so you get water views and an established feel.

Right beside Deer Lake Park on Royal Oak Avenue, Oaklands is a small low-rise pocket of mostly 1990s townhome complexes, with Royal Oak Station a short trip away. Buyers who like the lake area but want a low-rise scale tend to fit here.

Below Burke Mountain, Park Ridge Estates is an established 1990s pocket with houses south of David Avenue backing onto the Hyde Creek greenbelt. There’s no school inside the pocket, but families choose it for the greenbelt setting.

North of Lougheed Highway out to the Pitt River, Riverwood is Port Coquitlam’s northeast corner, built mostly in the 1980s and ’90s. It has a good mix of detached homes, townhouses and condos, with Terry Fox Secondary and Blakeburn Elementary in the area and Fremont Village and the Pitt River dike trails close by. Young families and first-time townhome buyers find a lot to like.
Within reach of Edmonds Station and the Tommy Douglas library branch, The Crest is an established East Burnaby house area with two elementary schools in the neighbourhood.

Uptown is New West’s plateau neighbourhood, with houses around the Sixth Street shops and Royal City Centre, and the 2024 təməsew̓txʷ Aquatic and Community Centre as its civic anchor. People like the scale and accept that there’s no SkyTrain station on the plateau itself.

Character houses on a slope define New West’s West End. Early-1900s homes sit beside plain post-war houses on steep streets dropping toward Fraser River views, and Twelfth Street’s heritage storefronts are the main shopping street.

Built on Eagle Mountain from the late 1980s on, Westwood Plateau is a master-planned community with single- family homes, duplexes, townhouses and apartments. Westwood Plateau Village at Parkway and Johnson handles shopping, and the Westwood Plateau Golf & Country Club and Eagle Mountain trails are right there. Families come for the schools, and it’s one of Coquitlam’s go-to areas for a newer home with nature at the door.
